lessons: Start with a vivid, surprising hook line – videos with non‑empty hook_line keep >1.0 of viewers at 10% while empty hooks drop below 0.5
Keep the hook concise; avoid long explanatory sentences in the first 10‑20% – biggest drops at 0.1‑0.2 are almost always plain facts
Use visual or sensory contrast (e.g., “older than the United States”, “looks like beef”) to sustain mid‑video retention – top videos with >0.6 at 50% use such hooks
Limit countdown or pause cues unless they build clear tension – the countdown flag shows mixed results and no consistent retention boost
Pose a curiosity‑driven question or paradox before the first factual block – high‑retention videos frame the hook as a question or mystery
Maintain a steady narrative pace after the hook; avoid inserting another dense fact block around 0.3‑0.4 where many drops occur
worst_moment_types: repetition of the same idea without new visual
dense technical detail without visual cue
countdown or pause without added tension
best_hook_types: surprising contrast or paradox (e.g., older than US, red‑meat fish)
vivid sensory image (e.g., ice water vs pepper fire)
question that challenges expectation (e.g., why do potatoes sprout in dents?)
short curiosity‑driven statement hinting at hidden mechanism
